summary:
Solmap is a layered 3D map of Mars for planning a human Marswalk. It opens on Jezero or Gale Crater and combines terrain elevation, slope hazards, CRISM mineral maps, the Perseverance and Curiosity routes, and the rovers’ sample sites, each with its photo and a short note on why it matters. Weather and radiation measured by NASA’s MEDA, REMS and RAD instruments are included where they exist.

The main feature is a safest-route planner. You pick a start and an end point, and it works out a route that avoids steep and unknown ground, and weighs roughness, radio line of sight, modelled radiation and science targets. It shows distance, walking time, climb, and the oxygen tanks needed.
details:
Project Description - SOLMAP

SOLMAP is an interactive platform for planning future human missions to Mars. It pulls information from several NASA missions into one easy-to-use view, so people can see and judge the Martian environment in one place.

It brings together surface height, terrain, minerals, temperature, radiation and the routes earlier rovers have driven. Each kind of information is its own layer on the map, so users can find possible routes, spot hazards, and pick destinations worth studying.

Instead of searching many separate sources, planners get one clear picture of the landscape. Planning a Mars mission means balancing astronaut safety, science, limited supplies and efficiency, and SOLMAP lets users weigh several factors at the same time. That can help planners choose safer routes, cut needless travel, pick the best science targets, and make the most of an astronaut's short time on the surface.

SOLMAP also shows that decades of robot exploration can keep helping future missions, because existing NASA data can be reused without new data collection for every planning decision.

How it works

SOLMAP is a web app that shows Mars in 3D, starting at Jezero and Gale Crater. Each type of information sits on its own layer: terrain height and steepness, CRISM minerals, rover routes, and sample sites with photos and short notes. Where instruments measured them, weather and radiation are included too.

The main feature is a safest-route planner that runs in the browser. You pick a start and an end point, and it finds the best path. It avoids ground that is too steep or has no data, and it also considers how hard the walk is, how rough the ground is, radio contact with the base, modelled radiation and science targets along the way. For each route it reports distance, walking time, climb, hazards, minerals, samples and the oxygen tanks needed. A mission report then appears on an Earth view, like a message sent back from Mars. Radiation at Jezero has not been measured, so it is shown as a labelled model, and the slope limits and oxygen use are stated assumptions.

What is the intended impact of your project?

We want SOLMAP to help make human exploration of Mars safer, more efficient, more productive for science, and open to more people.

For NASA and other space agencies, it could be a planning and decision tool that simplifies mission planning and may lower costs. For scientists, it makes it easier to explore how geology, geography and environment relate across Mars. For teachers, students and the public, it turns planetary science into something hands-on, using the same information real missions rely on.

In the end, we hope SOLMAP links robotic exploration to human exploration, so that what we have already discovered helps the next generation of Mars explorers.

How is your project creative?

Our creativity is in finding a new way to use data that already exists. NASA has gathered decades of information about Mars, but it is spread across many missions, instruments and archives. We started from the point of view of a future astronaut and asked what they would need to know before stepping onto the surface. That led us to build one connected platform that joins scientific discovery with practical planning.

We also widened what a map can do. SOLMAP does not only show where an astronaut can go. It helps users think about where they should go, why a place matters for science, and what dangers they might meet on the way.

We focused on five things:

- Astronaut safety: understanding hazards such as radiation, rough terrain and extreme temperatures.

- Scientific value: finding places that offer real chances for geology and new discoveries.

- Mission efficiency: planning routes that cut unnecessary travel, resource use and complexity.

- Accessibility: presenting complex data in a way that researchers, students and the public can understand.

- Data reliability: taking into account differences in resolution, coverage and collection dates, so old observations are not shown as current conditions.

These priorities guided our main goal: a platform that makes exploring Mars better informed, more practical, more inclusive and more meaningful for science.

Tools and technologies

- Languages: TypeScript and Python

- Front end: React 19 and Vite

- Mapping: ArcGIS Maps SDK for JavaScript, with a Mars coordinate system, 3D scenes and raster layers

- Data processing: Python scripts using GDAL, rasterio and NumPy

- Data sources: NASA rover data from Mars 2020 and MSL, CRISM minerals (NASA MRO), MEDA, REMS and RAD instrument data, NASA Mars Trek and GIBS imagery, plus USGS terrain models

- Methods: slope from elevation, A* route search, a walking-effort model (Minetti et al., 2002), and radio line-of-sight checks that account for the curve of the planet

- Hosting and teamwork: GitHub and Vercel

- Hardware: ordinary laptops

- AI assistance: an AI coding assistant (Claude) helped write and review parts of the code
